Q2Physics
subjectPhysics
chapterThermodynamics medium confidence
why this chapterThe answer (11RT) turns on the law of equipartition of energy, with 5/2 RT per mole for the diatomic O2 and 3/2 RT per mole for monatomic Ar; in this taxonomy that sits under Thermodynamics' 'Kinetic Theory of an Ideal Gas' and 'Specific Heat Capacity of Monoatomic, Diatomic, and Polyatomic Gases' topics.
subtopic 1Specific Heat Capacity of Monoatomic, Diatomic, and Polyatomic Gases
why this subtopicThe answer 11RT depends on the degrees of freedom of a diatomic gas (5, so U = 5/2 RT per mole for O2) and of a monatomic gas (3, so U = 3/2 RT per mole for Ar), giving 5RT + 6RT.
printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
A gas mixture consists of 2 moles of O2 and 4 moles of Ar at temperature T. Neglecting all vibrational modes, the total internal energy of the system is
  1. 4 RT
  2. 15 RT
  3. 9 RT
  4. 11 RT
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (4)
  1. U = n1f12RT + n2f22RT
  2. = 2 × 52RT + 4 × 32RT
  3. = 5 RT + 6 RT
  4. U = 11 RT

→ the working concludes: option 4

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 4 · high
  1. With vibrational modes neglected, O2 (diatomic) has f1 = 5 degrees of freedom and Ar (monatomic) has f2 = 3.
  2. Internal energy of O2: U1 = n1 f12 RT = 2 × 52 RT = 5 RT.
  3. Internal energy of Ar: U2 = n2 f22 RT = 4 × 32 RT = 6 RT.
  4. U = U1 + U2 = 5 RT + 6 RT = 11 RT, which is option 4.
printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict

stepsAssign degrees of freedom: O2 is diatomic with vibration neglected, f = 5; Ar is monatomic, f = 3 → Internal energy per mole = (f/2)RT, so O2 contributes 2 x (5/2)RT and Ar contributes 4 x (3/2)RT → Add: 5RT + 6RT
confusing options3 of 4 · options 2, 3, 4
15RT is exactly what you get using f = 5 for all six moles (forgetting that argon is monatomic) and 9RT is exactly f = 3 for all six moles (forgetting that oxygen is diatomic), so both wrong routes land on a printed option; only 4RT has no route behind it.

subjectPhysics
chapterModern Physics high confidence
why this chapterThe answer depends on the law of radioactive decay N = N0 e^(-lambda t) applied to two nuclides, which is listed under Modern Physics (topic 'Law of Radioactive Decay').
subtopic 1Law of Radioactive Decay
why this subtopicThe answer comes from applying the exponential decay law N = N0 e^(-lambda t) to both materials, giving N_B/N_A = e^(7 lambda t) and t = 1/(7 lambda).
printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
Radioactive material 'A' has decay constant '8λ' and material 'B' has decay constant 'λ'. Initially they have same number of nuclei. After what time, the ratio of number of nuclei of material 'B' to that 'A' will be 1e?
  1. 1λ
  2. 17λ
  3. 18λ
  4. 19λ
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (2)
  1. No option is correct
  2. If we take NANB = 1e
  3. Then
  4. NANB = e-8λ te-λ t
  5. 1e = e-7λ t
  6. -1 = -7λ t
  7. t = 17λ

→ the working concludes: option 2

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 2 · medium
  1. NA = N0 e-8λ t and NB = N0 e-λ t since both start with N0 nuclei.
  2. NBNA = e-λ te-8λ t = e7λ t.
  3. Setting e7λ t = 1e gives 7λ t = -1, i.e. a negative time, because NB/NA ≥ 1 for all t ≥ 0.
  4. The physically meaningful reading is NANB = e-7λ t = 1e, so 7λ t = 1.
  5. t = 17λ, which is option 2.
printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict
22 mediumagree
difficultymedium · 3 steps
stepsWrite N = N0 e^(-lambda t) for both, with the same N0 → Form the ratio so the exponents subtract: the difference of decay constants is 8lambda - lambda = 7lambda → Set the exponential equal to 1/e, so the exponent magnitude is 1, and solve t = 1/(7lambda)
confusing options3 of 4 · options 2, 3, 4
1/(9lambda) is what you get ADDING the two decay constants instead of subtracting them, and 1/(8lambda) is what you get using only the faster material's constant and ignoring B altogether -- both are one keystroke away from the right route.
why this bandThree short steps, but the options are built so that every way of combining 8lambda and lambda is printed: subtract gives 7, add gives 9, use one alone gives 8 or 1, so elimination is useless and the candidate has to actually handle the exponent difference.
the catchAs printed the ratio asked for is B to A, and since B decays slower that ratio grows above 1 and can never equal 1/e -- a careful candidate loses time on the sign before settling for the intended magnitude.
noteThe stem's 'ratio of B to A = 1/e' gives a negative time if taken literally; rated as the intended magnitude calculation, with the sign confusion counted as a time cost rather than as damage.

Q4Physics
subjectPhysics
chapterMechanical Properties of Fluids high confidence
why this chapterThe answer comes from balancing hydrostatic pressure (rho g h) of the oil column against the water column at the same level in a U-tube, which is hydrostatics in fluids.
subtopic 1Problems on Hydrostatics
why this subtopicThe answer comes from equating the hydrostatic pressure (h rho g) of the 140 mm oil column with that of the 130 mm water column at the same level in a U-tube open to the atmosphere, giving rho_oil = 1000 x 130/140 = 928 kg m^-3.
printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
A U tube with both ends open to the atmosphere, is partially filled with water. Oil, which is immiscible with water, is poured into one side until it stands at a distance of 10 mm above the water level on the other side. Meanwhile the water rises by 65 mm from its original level (see diagram). The density of the oil is
  1. 650 kg m-3
  2. 425 kg m-3
  3. 800 kg m-3
  4. 928 kg m-3
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (4)
  1. hoil ρoil g = hwater ρwater g
  2. 140 × ρoil = 130 × ρwater
  3. ρoil = 1314 × 1000 kg/m3
  4. ρoil = 928 kg m-3

→ the working concludes: option 4

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 4 · high
  1. Water rises 65 mm on the right, so the oil-water interface on the left falls 65 mm to level B.
  2. Water column above level B on the right: hw = 65 + 65 = 130 mm.
  3. Oil column above B on the left: ho = 130 + 10 = 140 mm.
  4. Equal pressure at level B: ρo g ho = ρw g hw.
  5. ρo = 1000 × 130140 ≈ 928 kg m-3, which is option 4.
printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict
44 highagree
difficultyhard · 4 steps
stepsRead the figure: the right-hand water level rose 65 mm, so the left-hand water level fell 65 mm and the water surfaces now differ by 130 mm → Get the oil column length: it reaches from the depressed left water surface up to a point 10 mm above the right-hand water level, i.e. 65 + 65 + 10 = 140 mm → Balance pressures at the oil-water interface in the left arm: rho_oil x 140 = rho_water x 130 → Solve with rho_water = 1000 and evaluate 1000 x 130/140
confusing options3 of 4 · options 1, 3, 4 · long to execute
650 is exactly 1000 x 65/100, the answer you get by pairing the single printed 65 mm against a 100 mm oil column instead of doubling the 65 and adding the 10; 800 is the round ratio you get from a 10:8 column guess; only the careful 140-versus-130 bookkeeping lands on 928.
why this bandFour steps and the hard part is not the hydrostatics -- it is the geometry: the 65 mm rise on one side means a 65 mm fall on the other, so the two columns are 140 and 130 and not 75 and 65, and the plausible round number 650 is sitting there for anyone who counts the 65 once.
the catchThe figure gives 65 mm once but it has to be used twice, and the answer is a near-unity ratio (130/140), so the distractors 650 and 800 look far more like 'a density' than the correct value does.

Q5Physics
subjectPhysics
chapterMagnetic Effect of Electric Current high confidence
why this chapterThe answer turns on the work done in rotating a current-carrying coil (magnetic dipole m = NIA) by 180 degrees in a uniform magnetic field, W = 2NIAB, which is taught under torque/potential energy of a current loop in a magnetic field.
subtopic 1Work Done or Potential Energy of a Current-Carrying Loop in a Uniform Magnetic Field
why this subtopicThe answer is the work done in rotating a current-carrying coil by 180 degrees in a uniform field, W = 2NIAB, which is the potential-energy change of a current loop in a uniform magnetic field.
printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
A 250-Turn rectangular coil of length 2.1 cm and width 1.25 cm carries a current of 85 μA and subjected to a magnetic field of strength 0.85 T. Work done for rotating the coil by 180° against the torque is
  1. 9.1 μJ
  2. 4.55 μJ
  3. 2.3 μJ
  4. 1.15 μJ
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (1)
  1. W = MB (cosθ1 - cosθ2)
  2. When it is rotated by angle 180° then
  3. W = 2MB
  4. W = 2 (NIA)B
  5. = 2 × 250 × 85 × 10-6[1.25 × 2.1 × 10-4] × 85 × 10-2
  6. = 9.1 μJ

→ the working concludes: option 1

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 1 · medium
  1. Area of the coil: A = 2.1×10-2 m × 1.25×10-2 m = 2.625×10-4 m2.
  2. Magnetic moment: m = NIA = 250 × 85×10-6 × 2.625×10-4 = 5.578×10-6 A m2.
  3. Work to rotate from θ = 0° to θ = 180°: W = mB(cos 0° - cos 180°) = 2mB.
  4. W = 2 × 5.578×10-6 × 0.85 = 9.48×10-6 J ≈ 9.5 μJ.
  5. The nearest option is 9.1 μJ, which is option 1.
printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict
11 mediumagree
difficultyhard · 4 steps
stepsArea from cm to m^2: 2.1 x 1.25 cm^2 = 2.625 cm^2 = 2.625e-4 m^2 → Magnetic moment M = NIA with N = 250 and I = 85 microamp → Work to turn 180 degrees against the torque: W = MB(cos0 - cos180) = 2MB, not MB → Multiply through and convert to microjoules
confusing options3 of 4 · options 1, 2, 3 · long to execute
The options are a factor-of-two ladder -- 9.1, 4.55, 2.3, 1.15 -- so 4.55 is exactly MB (the dropped factor of 2 from the 180-degree turn) and 2.3 is exactly MB/2 (using the (1/2)MB form), meaning every common slip has its own printed home.
why this bandHard on both spines: four steps including a cm-squared to m-squared conversion and a micro-amp to micro-joule chain, and the options are deliberately in 2:1 ratios so that forgetting the 180-degree turn is worth 2MB versus MB lands you on option 2 with no arithmetic warning at all.
the catchThe factor of two in W = 2MB for a 180-degree reversal is the entire question, and the option set is built so that dropping it is indistinguishable from getting it right.

printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
The de-Broglie wavelength of a neutron in thermal equilibrium with heavy water at a temperature T (Kelvin) and mass m, is
  1. hmkT
  2. h3mkT
  3. 2h3mkT
  4. 2hmkT
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (2)
  1. de-Broglie wavelength
  2. λ = hmv
  3. = h2m(KE)
  4. = h2m(32kT)
  5. λ = h3mkT

→ the working concludes: option 2

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 2 · high
  1. A neutron in thermal equilibrium at temperature T has mean kinetic energy E = 32kT.
  2. Momentum p = 2mE = 2m · 32kT = 3mkT.
  3. de Broglie wavelength λ = hp = h3mkT, which is option 2.

Q7Physics
subjectPhysics
chapterLaws of Motion high confidence
why this chapterThe answer turns on the fact that, on a smooth horizontal table, the string tension alone supplies the centripetal force, so the net force towards the centre is T, which is the dynamics of circular motion taught in Laws of Motion.
subtopic 1Tension in String in Circular Motion
why this subtopicThe answer rests on the fact that, for a particle whirled in a horizontal circle on a smooth table, the string tension T alone supplies the net centripetal force.
printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
One end of string of length l is connected to a particle of mass 'm' and the other end is connected to a small peg on a smooth horizontal table. If the particle moves in circle with speed 'v', the net force on the particle (directed towards center) will be (T represents the tension in the string)
  1. T
  2. T+mv2l
  3. T-mv2l
  4. Zero
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (1)
  1. Centripetal force (mv2l) is provided by tension so the net force will be equal to tension i.e., T.

→ the working concludes: option 1

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 1 · high
  1. Vertically, the normal reaction balances gravity: N = mg, so these give no net force.
  2. The table is smooth, so there is no friction; the only horizontal force on the particle is the tension T along the string towards the peg.
  3. Hence the net force towards the centre is Fnet = T (which equals mv2l), which is option 1.
printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict
11 highagree
difficultymedium · 1 step
stepsIn the ground (inertial) frame the only horizontal force on the particle is the string tension, so the net inward force IS T (and equals mv^2/l) -- no centrifugal term belongs in the sum
confusing options3 of 4 · options 1, 3, 4
T - mv^2/l is exactly what you write if you add the centrifugal pseudo-force in the lab frame, and 'Zero' is where that same wrong route ends once you notice T = mv^2/l, so the two commonest misconceptions are both printed and option 4 even looks like the 'clever' answer.
why this bandOne line of reasoning, but three of the four options have a route: the frame confusion that produces T - mv^2/l resolves to zero, so a candidate who mixes frames finds two mutually supporting wrong answers and never doubts them -- the question is decided by the frame choice, not by any calculation.
the catchMixing the rotating and inertial frames is the trap, and the option set rewards it twice over (options 3 and 4 are the same mistake at two stages).

printed in the booklet
publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
Figure shows a circuit contains three identical resistors with resistance R = 9.0 Ω each, two identical inductors with inductance L = 2.0 mH each, and an ideal battery with emf ε = 18 V. The current 'i' through the battery just after the switch closed is
  1. 2 mA
  2. 0.2 A
  3. 2 A
  4. 0 ampere
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (3)
  1. At t = 0, no current flows through R1 and R3

PProcess IaAdiabatic
QProcess IIbIsobaric

  1. Process I is a vertical line on the P-V diagram, so V is constant: isochoric, P → c.

  3. Process III runs along the 500 K curve, so T is constant: isothermal, R → d.
  4. Process IV is a horizontal line, so P is constant: isobaric, S → b.
  5. P → c, Q → a, R → d, S → b is option 2.

READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
A capacitor is charged by a battery. The battery is removed and another identical uncharged capacitor is connected in parallel. The total electrostatic energy of resulting system
  1. Increases by a factor of 4
  2. Decreases by a factor of 2
  3. Remains the same
  4. Increases by a factor of 2
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (2)
  1. Charge on capacitor
  2. q = CV
  3. when it is connected with another uncharged capacitor.
  4. Vc = q1 + q2C1 + C2 = q + 0C + C
  5. Vc = V2
  6. Initial energy
  7. Ui = 12CV2
  8. Final energy
  9. Uf = 12C(V2)2 + 12C(V2)2
  10. = CV24
  11. Loss of energy = Ui - Uf
  12. = CV24
  13. i.e. decreases by a factor (2)

→ the working concludes: option 2

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 2 · high
  1. With the battery removed, the charge Q on the first capacitor is conserved; initial energy U = Q22C.
  2. Connecting an identical uncharged capacitor in parallel gives C' = C + C = 2C with the same total charge Q.
  3. U' = Q22C' = Q24C = U2.
  4. The energy decreases by a factor of 2, which is option 2.

READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
A physical quantity of the dimensions of length that can be formed out of c, G and e24πε0 is [c is velocity of light, G is universal constant of gravitation and e is charge]
  1. 1c2[Ge24πε0]12
  2. c2[Ge24πε0]12
  3. 1c2[e2G4πε0]12
  4. 1cGe24πε0
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (1)
  1. Let e24πε0 = A = ML3T-2
  2. l = CxGy(A)z
  3. L = [LT-1]x [M-1L3T-2]y [ML3T-2]z
  4. -y + z = 0 ⇒ y = z ...(i)
  5. x + 3y + 3z = 1 ...(ii)
  6. -x - 4z = 0 ...(iii)
  7. From (i), (ii) & (iii)
  8. z = y = 12, x = -2

→ the working concludes: option 1

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 1 · high
  1. From Coulomb's law F = e24πε0 r2, so [e24πε0] = [F r2] = M L3 T-2.
  2. From F = G m2r2, [G] = M-1 L3 T-2.
  3. [Ge24πε0] = M-1L3T-2 · M L3 T-2 = L6 T-4.
  4. [Ge24πε0]1/2 = L3 T-2.
  5. [c2] = L2 T-2, so 1c2[Ge24πε0]1/2 = L3T-2L2T-2 = L, which is option 1.

publisher’s solution, as printed
READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
If θ1 and θ2 be the apparent angles of dip observed in two vertical planes at right angles to each other, then the true angle of dip θ is given by
  1. cot2θ = cot2θ1 + cot2θ2
  2. tan2θ = tan2θ1 + tan2θ2
  3. cot2θ = cot2θ1 - cot2θ2
  4. tan2θ = tan2θ1 - tan2θ2
The publisher's solutionprinted answer (1)
  1. cot2θ = cot2θ1 + cot2θ2

→ the working concludes: option 1

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 1 · high
  1. Let the first vertical plane make angle α with the magnetic meridian; the second is at 90° - α.
  2. In the first plane the horizontal component is Hcosα, so tanθ1 = VHcosα, i.e. cotθ1 = HcosαV.
  3. In the second plane the horizontal component is Hsinα, so cotθ2 = HsinαV.
  4. Squaring and adding: cot2θ1 + cot2θ2 = H2(cos2α + sin2α)V2 = H2V2.
  5. True dip satisfies cotθ = HV, so cot2θ = cot2θ1 + cot2θ2, which is option 1.

Which is the incorrect statement?
  1. FeO0.98 has non stoichiometric metal deficiency defect

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 4 · high
  1. FeO0.98 has fewer Fe than O ions, a non-stoichiometric metal deficiency defect, so option 1 is correct.
  2. Schottky defect removes cation-anion pairs from the lattice, so mass per unit volume falls and density decreases; option 2 is correct.
  3. NaCl(s) is an insulator, Si a semiconductor, Ag a conductor and quartz piezoelectric; option 3 is correct.

  4. ∴ [C2O42-] = 2.2×10-42 M = 1.1×10-4 M

printed solution, as in the booklet
Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 4 · high
  1. Ag2C2O4 ⇌ 2Ag+ + C2O42-, so [C2O42-] = 12[Ag+].
  2. [C2O42-] = 2.2 × 10-42 = 1.1 × 10-4 mol L-1.
  3. Ksp = [Ag+]2[C2O42-].
  4. [Ag+]2 = (2.2 × 10-4)2 = 4.84 × 10-8.

      1. Inability of ns2 electrons of the valence shell to participate in bonding on moving down the group in heavier p-block elements is called inert pair effect

      3. Sn(IV) is more stable than Sn(II)
      4. ∴ Pb(IV) is easily reduced to Pb(II)

      1. The reluctance of ns2 electrons to bond (inert pair effect) grows down group 14, so the +2 state gets more stable relative to +4.

      3. For lead the +2 state is the more stable one, so Pb4+ + 2e- → Pb2+ happens readily, making Pb4+ an oxidising agent.
      4. This matches option 1.

      READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
      A gas is allowed to expand in a well insulated container against a constant external pressure of 2.5 atm from an initial volume of 2.50 L to a final volume of 4.50 L. The change in internal energy Δ U of the gas in joules will be
      1. 1136.25 J
      2. -500 J
      3. -505 J
      4. +505 J
      The publisher's solutionprinted answer (3)
      1. Δ U = q + w
      2. For adiabatic process, q = 0
      3. ∴ Δ U = w
      4. = -P·Δ V
      5. = -2.5 atm × (4.5 - 2.5) L
      6. = -2.5 × 2 L-atm
      7. = -5 × 101.3 J
      8. = -506.5 J
      9. ≈ -505 J

      → the working concludes: option 3

      printed solution, as in the booklet
      Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 3 · high
      1. The container is well insulated, so the process is adiabatic: q = 0.
      2. First law: Δ U = q + w = w.
      3. Work against constant external pressure: w = -Pext(V2 - V1) = -2.5 atm × (4.50 - 2.50) L = -5.0 L atm.
      4. Convert: -5.0 L atm × 101 J L-1 atm-1 ≈ -505 J.
      5. Δ U = -505 J, which is option 3.

          2. (II) N2 + O2 ⇌ 2NO; K2 = [NO]2[N2][O2]
          3. (III) H2 + 12O2 ⟶ H2O; K3 = [H2O][H2][O2]1/2
          4. (II + 3 × III – II) will give
          5. 2NH3 + 52O2 K⇌ 2NO + 3H2O;
          6. ∴ K = K2 × K33 / K1

          1. Reverse reaction 1: 2NH3 ⇌ N2 + 3H2, constant 1K1.
          2. Keep reaction 2: N2 + O2 ⇌ 2NO, constant K2.
          3. Multiply reaction 3 by 3: 3H2 + 32O2 ⇌ 3H2O, constant K33.
          4. Add the three: N2 and 3H2 cancel, O2 totals 1 + 32 = 52, giving 2NH3 + 52O2 ⇌ 2NO + 3H2O.
          5. Constants multiply on adding reactions: K = K2 K33K1, which is option 2.

          2. (i) Condensation of DNA so that chromosomes become visible occurs during early to mid-prophase.
          3. (ii) Nuclear membrane disassembly begins at late prophase or transition to metaphase.
          4. (iii) Arrangement of chromosomes at equator occurs during metaphase, called congression.
          5. (iv) Centromere division or splitting occurs during anaphase forming daughter chromosomes.
          6. (v) Segregation also occurs during anaphase as daughter chromosomes separate and move to opposite poles.

          READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
          During DNA replication, Okazaki fragments are used to elongate
          1. The leading strand towards replication fork
          2. The lagging strand towards replication fork
          3. The leading strand away from replication fork
          4. The lagging strand away from the replication fork
          The publisher's solutionprinted answer (4)
          1. Two DNA polymerase molecules work simultaneous at the DNA fork, one on the leading strand and the other on the lagging strand.
          2. Each Okazaki fragment is synthesized by DNA polymerase at lagging strand in 5' → 3' direction.
          3. New Okazaki fragments appear as the replication fork opens further.
          4. As the first Okazaki fragment appears away from the replication fork, the direction of elongation would be away from replication fork.

          → the working concludes: option 4

          printed solution, as in the booklet
          Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 4 · medium
          1. Okazaki fragments are formed only on the lagging strand; the leading strand is synthesised continuously, which rules out options 1 and 3.
          2. DNA polymerase adds nucleotides only in the 5' → 3' direction, and on the lagging strand this direction points away from the replication fork.
          3. So each Okazaki fragment elongates the lagging strand away from the replication fork, which is option 4.

          why this chapterThe answer (33) depends on the triplet genetic code and how a single-base deletion causes a frameshift that alters every codon from the deleted position (codon 301) to the end (codon 333), which is taught under the genetic code and effect of mutation on it.
          subtopic 1Effect of Mutation on Genetic Code

          printed in the booklet
          publisher’s solution, as printed
          READ FROM THE IMAGE by b3-question-reader
          If there are 999 bases in an RNA that codes for a protein with 333 amino acids, and the base at position 901 is deleted such that the length of the RNA becomes 998 bases, how many codons will be altered?
          1. 1
          2. 11
          3. 33
          4. 333
          The publisher's solutionprinted answer (3)
          1. If deletion occurs at 901st position the remaining 98 bases specifying for 33 codons of amino acids will be altered.

          → the working concludes: option 3

          printed solution, as in the booklet
          Solved independently (answer withheld)AI: 3 · high
          1. A protein of 333 amino acids is coded by 333 × 3 = 999 bases.
          2. Base 901 is the first base of codon 9003 + 1 = 301.
          3. Deleting it causes a frameshift from codon 301 to the last codon 333.
          4. Codons altered = 333 - 301 + 1 = 33, which is option 3.
          printed in the bookletsolved independentlyverdict
          33 highagree
          difficultyhard · 3 steps
          stepsSee that deleting one base is a frameshift, not a single substitution, so everything downstream reads in a new frame → Locate base 901 in the reading frame: 900/3 = 300 complete codons, so base 901 opens codon 301 → Count codons 301 to 333 inclusive and allow for the now-incomplete last triplet to get the number altered
          confusing options3 of 4 · options 1, 2, 3 · long to execute
          Option 1 is exactly what a candidate picks who treats a deletion like a point substitution; option 3 is the frameshift count done right; option 2 is the near-miss that an off-by-one or a 1/3-of-33 slip produces, and option 4 (all 333) is the only one that is plainly a different kind of error.
          why this bandHard: this is biology asking for arithmetic reasoning rather than a line of NCERT - three linked steps (frameshift insight, locating 901 in the frame, then counting to the stop) with an off-by-one waiting at the 900/901 boundary, and the option set contains both the naive single-codon answer and the correct downstream count, so a candidate who does not actually reason it through has no way to guess.
          the catchThe frameshift insight is not signposted - the stem's mention of 998 bases invites a length calculation instead - and the live options are the exact products of the two commonest wrong routes.

          1. Thalassemia results from mutation or deletion that reduces or stops synthesis of α or β globin chains, i.e. a quantitative problem: fewer globin molecules are made.
          2. Sickle cell anemia results from a single substitution (Glu → Val at the 6th position of β-globin), i.e. a qualitative problem: a faulty globin is made.
          3. So options 1, 2 and 4 are false and option 3 is correct.
